title: What a transaction promises: ACID and isolation levels
goal: By the end you can say what each ACID letter promises and what it doesn't, tell a single-object write from a multi-object transaction, predict what Read Committed, Repeatable Read and Serializable do about each anomaly in PostgreSQL (and why the same names mean other things in Oracle and MySQL), and write a retry loop that stays safe when a commit acknowledgement is lost.

warmup.q: Ivy has two accounts with 5,000 each, and her total must stay at or above zero. Two withdrawals of 8,000, one from each account, run at the same moment. Each is a REPEATABLE READ transaction that reads her total, then updates its own account. What does PostgreSQL do?
options: The second transaction waits for the first, then sees the new total and refuses
The second COMMIT fails with a serialization error
Both commit, and her total ends at -6,000
The second UPDATE fails because the first one changed the total
warmup.why: Each transaction reads its own snapshot, taken before either wrote, so both see 10,000. They update different rows, so neither waits for a row lock, and Repeatable Read only reports two transactions that change the same row. Both commit: write skew. A serialization error would come at SERIALIZABLE, which tracks what each transaction read.

sections.h: A transaction makes several changes count as one
sections.body:
The Replication and Partitioning tracks put copies and pieces of your data on many machines. This track asks what happens when one piece of work changes several of those records and something fails halfway, or two pieces of work touch the same records at once. It starts on one machine, with what a transaction promises, and gets to transactions across machines in lesson 7.

One write to one row is already safe. When PostgreSQL updates a row, no other session sees half of it, and a crash halfway leaves the old version or the new one, never a mix: the write-ahead log makes the write atomic, and a row lock keeps a second writer out until the first is done. Every serious storage engine promises that for a single object, and `UPDATE accounts SET balance_minor = balance_minor - 2000 WHERE account_id = 109` gets it, read and write included.

Trouble starts with two objects. Moving 2,000 from Ivy's account 109 to her account 209 takes two statements:

```sql
UPDATE accounts SET balance_minor = balance_minor - 2000 WHERE account_id = 109;
UPDATE accounts SET balance_minor = balance_minor + 2000 WHERE account_id = 209;
```

If the service dies between them, because a pod restarts or a connection drops, 109 has lost 2,000 and 209 never got it. The window is a few milliseconds, and a service that makes a million transfers a day will land in it now and then. Any change that must touch several places in step has the same window: a payment and its ledger entries, the cached `balance_minor` and the entries it sums, a row and its index entries. A key-value store's multi-put doesn't close it on its own either: some keys can succeed while others fail.

A **transaction** closes the window. `BEGIN` starts one. Every change after it is provisional: `COMMIT` makes all of them permanent at once, and `ROLLBACK` throws all of them away. If the connection drops or the server crashes before `COMMIT`, PostgreSQL rolls back for you.

The commit is a single event. On `COMMIT`, PostgreSQL writes one commit record to its write-ahead log and, with the default `synchronous_commit = on`, waits for it to reach the disk before it replies. Until that record is on disk, the transaction never happened; after it, all of it did. The Storage engines track builds this log in "Write-ahead logging and crash recovery". An error inside a transaction fails the whole transaction: PostgreSQL refuses every later statement with `current transaction is aborted`, and a `COMMIT` at the end turns into a `ROLLBACK`.

Outside `BEGIN`, every statement is its own transaction. psql works that way, and so does JDBC, where a new `Connection` has `autoCommit = true`:

```kotlin
conn.autoCommit = false                 // statements now join one transaction
try {
    debit.executeUpdate()               // 109 - 2000
    credit.executeUpdate()              // 209 + 2000
    conn.commit()                       // both become permanent together
} catch (e: SQLException) {
    conn.rollback()                     // neither does
    throw e
}
```

Keep one picture for the rest of the track. A transaction works on a private draft: it reads the database as it was at some moment, its writes go into the draft, and `COMMIT` publishes the whole draft in one step.

try.title: A transfer that fails halfway
steps: Start the database if it is not running (`docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait`, from the `labs` folder). Open psql: `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz -d course`.
Run the block one statement at a time. The second UPDATE sets a status the CHECK constraint forbids, so the transfer fails halfway.
Before the last SELECT, predict: does 109 show 3,000 or 5,000?

code.title: psql, database course

try.expect:
Inside the transaction, 109 already shows 3,000. Then the second UPDATE fails, and from that moment the transaction refuses everything (output trimmed):

```postgresql
UPDATE 1
 account_id | balance_minor
------------+---------------
        109 |          3000
        209 |          5000
(2 rows)

ERROR:  new row for relation "accounts" violates check constraint "accounts_status_check"
DETAIL:  Failing row contains (209, customer, 9, null, USD, open, 7000, 2026-01-20 11:06:00+00).
ERROR:  current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block
ROLLBACK
 account_id | balance_minor
------------+---------------
        109 |          5000
        209 |          5000
(2 rows)
```

`COMMIT` printed `ROLLBACK`: PostgreSQL will not commit a transaction that had an error. The debit of 109 is gone with it, so no money vanished. Nothing needs cleaning up.

sections.h: ACID is four promises, and only one of them is about concurrency
sections.body:
Theo Härder and Andreas Reuter coined "ACID" in 1983 for the four promises a transaction makes. Today vendors use it mostly as a label, so it pays to know what each letter buys:

| Letter | It sounds like | What you actually get |
|---|---|---|
| Atomicity | all or nothing | abortability: if anything fails before COMMIT, every write of the transaction is undone |
| Consistency | the data stays valid | your rules, enforced only where you declared them: keys, foreign keys, CHECK, UNIQUE |
| Isolation | concurrent transactions don't interfere | whatever your isolation level allows; PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server default to Read Committed |
| Durability | committed data survives | the commit record is on disk, or on replicas, with fine print |

Atomicity is the easy one to misread. In Kotlin, "atomic" means other threads can't see a half-done step. In ACID that job belongs to I. A is about faults: the database can throw a transaction away, which is what lets your code retry it.

Consistency belongs to you. In the Try it, PostgreSQL rejects a refund of 0, because a CHECK says `amount_minor > 0`, and accepts a refund that brings payment 5's refunds to 58,000 on a 48,000 payment, because nobody declared that rule. The database keeps exactly the invariants you told it about.

Durability has fine print. With PostgreSQL's defaults, COMMIT returns only after its commit record is flushed. Set `synchronous_commit = off` and a crash can lose the last few commits. Replicas help until a failover lands on one that lagged (the Replication track). SSDs have acknowledged flushes they never did, and one firmware bug failed drives after exactly 32,768 hours of use. In 2026 Jepsen showed MariaDB Galera Cluster losing acknowledged commits when every node crashed in quick succession with `innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit=0`, a setting MariaDB's documentation called safer. Durability lowers the risk: keep a disk, replicas and backups.

Isolation is the hard part, and the rest of this track is about it. "ACID compliant" usually means atomic, durable commits at a default isolation level well below "as if you were alone". When Jepsen tested ParticleDB in 2026, its home page said "Full ACID" and the text below said snapshot isolation. So ask a different question of every database: which anomalies does its default level allow?

try.title: What the database enforces, and what it doesn't
steps: Open psql: `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz -d course`. Start the database if it is not running (`docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait`, from the `labs` folder).
Check the defaults that the letters D and I depend on, then look at payment 5 and its refunds.
Run the block one statement at a time. Before each INSERT, predict whether PostgreSQL accepts it.

code.title: psql, database course

try.expect:
The defaults are `read committed` and `on`. Payment 5 is 48000 with 18000 refunded. The first INSERT succeeds, and the sum shows the broken rule (output trimmed):

```postgresql
INSERT 0 1
 refunded
----------
    58000
(1 row)

ERROR:  new row for relation "refunds" violates check constraint "refunds_amount_minor_check"
DETAIL:  Failing row contains (8, 5, 0, customer_request, 2026-11-08 05:33:14.851113+00).
ROLLBACK
```

PostgreSQL refunded 58,000 on a 48,000 payment without a word, because no constraint says it can't, and refused the refund of 0, because a CHECK does. The ROLLBACK removes the refund that did go in. The refund_id in the DETAIL (8 here) keeps climbing on every run: a sequence hands out numbers outside the transaction and never takes them back.

sections.h: Isolation levels decide which moment a transaction reads, and the names differ by vendor
sections.body:
A transaction never reads another transaction's draft. PostgreSQL manages that without making readers wait, because an `UPDATE` never overwrites a row in place: it writes a new version and keeps the old one for a while (lesson 4 opens that machinery up). A **snapshot** decides which versions a statement sees: everything committed before the snapshot was taken, nothing committed after, and nothing uncommitted. So PostgreSQL never gives you a dirty read, a value from a transaction that hasn't committed. The isolation level decides when the snapshot is taken.

Read Committed, PostgreSQL's default, takes a new snapshot at the start of every statement. Inside one transaction, two identical SELECTs can disagree: read 109's balance (5,000), another session debits it and commits, read again (4,000). That is a non-repeatable read. When the set of rows changes instead, say a new ledger entry appears in a `sum(amount_minor)`, it's a phantom (lesson 3).

Repeatable Read takes one snapshot, at the first statement, and keeps it to the end, so every read agrees. This is **snapshot isolation**. It also changes writes: if a row you update was changed and committed by someone else after your snapshot, PostgreSQL refuses with `could not serialize access due to concurrent update` (SQLSTATE 40001), because you'd be overwriting a version you've never seen. That stops the lost update, the subject of lesson 2.

| PostgreSQL | Read Committed | Repeatable Read | Serializable |
|---|---|---|---|
| dirty read | never | never | never |
| non-repeatable read, phantom | yes | no | no |
| lost update | yes | error 40001 | error 40001 |
| write skew | yes | yes | error 40001 |

The names come from the SQL standard, which defines its levels by three phenomena described in English, in definitions older than snapshot isolation. Each vendor fitted its own engine to the names. Hermitage, Martin Kleppmann's suite that runs the same interleavings against many databases, shows the result:

| Name | Default in | What it really is |
|---|---|---|
| READ COMMITTED | PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server | a fresh snapshot (or lock) per statement |
| REPEATABLE READ | PostgreSQL | snapshot isolation |
| REPEATABLE READ | MySQL (InnoDB) | weaker than snapshot isolation: lost updates get through |
| SERIALIZABLE | Oracle | snapshot isolation: write skew gets through |
| SERIALIZABLE | PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server | serializable |

MySQL's row surprises people most. In 2023, Jepsen ran a single healthy MySQL 8.0.34 node at its default REPEATABLE READ and found 198 lost updates in 446 transactions in one test, plus transactions that read the same row twice and got two answers. InnoDB's snapshot covers plain SELECTs; an UPDATE works on the newest committed row instead. The level's name tells you the vendor, not the guarantee.

try.title: The same SELECT twice, at two levels
steps: Open two terminals in the `labs` folder and run psql in both: `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz -d course`. Call them A and B. Start the database if it is not running (`docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait`, from the `labs` folder).
Run the Read Committed block: A reads, B debits (B is in autocommit, so its UPDATE commits at once), A reads again. Do A's two reads agree?
Run the Repeatable Read block. Predict A's second SELECT, then A's UPDATE.

code.title: psql, two sessions on database course

try.expect:
At Read Committed, A's two SELECTs disagree inside one transaction: 5000, then 4000, because B's debit committed in between. At Repeatable Read both SELECTs return 4000, though B has moved the balance to 3000, and A's own UPDATE is refused:

```postgresql
-- A
 balance_minor
---------------
          4000
(1 row)

ERROR:  could not serialize access due to concurrent update
40001
ROLLBACK
```

`\echo :SQLSTATE` prints the error code of the last statement, the code your Kotlin code would see in `SQLException.sqlState`. After A's ROLLBACK the balance is 3000 (both of B's debits); the last statement puts 5,000 back.

sections.h: Write skew breaks a rule that spans two rows
sections.body:
Ivy (customer 9) has accounts 109 and 209 with 5,000 each. The bank lets one account go negative as long as her total stays at or above zero. Two withdrawals of 8,000 arrive at the same moment, one on each account. Each transaction checks the rule and then writes:

```sql
BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
SELECT sum(balance_minor) FROM accounts WHERE customer_id = 9;                    -- 10000: allowed
UPDATE accounts SET balance_minor = balance_minor - 8000 WHERE account_id = 109;  -- B: 209
COMMIT;
```

Both read 10,000 from snapshots taken before either wrote. A updates 109, B updates 209. They change different rows, so neither waits for a row lock, and Repeatable Read finds no row that both changed. Both commit. Ivy's total is -6,000.

This is **write skew**. Each transaction read rows that the other one then changed, and each write was correct for the data its transaction saw. Run in either order, the second withdrawal would have seen 2,000 and refused. Run together, they produced a state that no order of the two could produce. Any rule that reads rows it doesn't write has this hole: a merchant's daily limit enforced across several terminals, two bookings of one meeting room, two refunds that each check the payment's remaining amount.

Repeatable Read doesn't catch it, and Oracle's `SERIALIZABLE` doesn't either: Hermitage shows Oracle's highest level is snapshot isolation, which stops lost updates and lets write skew through. Oracle code that enforces a limit across rows with a read and then a write needs an explicit lock, whatever the level is called. Lesson 3 is about the harder cases, where the rows a rule depends on don't exist yet.

The stepper runs the two withdrawals at each level, then shows the two fixes: Serializable, in the next section, and a lock on the rows the rule reads.

try.title: Overdraw Ivy at Repeatable Read
steps: Open two terminals in the `labs` folder and run psql in both: `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz -d course`. Call them A and B. Start the database if it is not running (`docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait`, from the `labs` folder).

code.title: psql, two sessions on database course

Both checks print 10000. Neither UPDATE waits, both print `UPDATE 1`, and both COMMITs succeed:

```postgresql

------------+---------------
```

Ivy's total is -6,000, at Repeatable Read, with no error anywhere. The last statement puts both accounts back at 5,000.

refs.title: Hermitage: testing transaction isolation levels (PostgreSQL, Oracle, MySQL and others)

sections.h: Serializable catches write skew, and a retry has to be safe to repeat

try.title: Serializable with a retry, and a retry that can't charge twice
steps: Open two terminals in the `labs` folder and run psql in both: `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz -d course`. Call them A and B. Start the database if it is not running (`docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait`, from the `labs` folder).
Run part 1, switching at each comment. Which COMMIT fails, and with what SQLSTATE? Run B's retry and read its total.
Part 2 needs one session. It inserts the same 42.00 charge twice, as a client would after a lost COMMIT reply: first without a key, then with a fixed `payment_uid`. Predict the row counts.

code.title: psql, two sessions on database course

try.expect:
In part 1, everything up to A's COMMIT looks exactly like the Repeatable Read run. Then B's COMMIT fails:

```postgresql
-- B
ERROR:  could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions
DETAIL:  Reason code: Canceled on identification as a pivot, during commit attempt.
HINT:  The transaction might succeed if retried.
40001
-- B, retrying
  sum
------
 2000
(1 row)
```

The retry sees A's withdrawal and a total of 2,000, so B refuses. In part 2 the two keyless inserts return two new ids (38 and 39 on a fresh database): the customer was charged twice. With the key, the first insert returns a new id and the second returns nothing:

```postgresql
 payment_id
------------
(0 rows)

INSERT 0 0
 count
-------
     3
(1 row)
```

Three rows: two from the keyless retry, one from the keyed pair. The last statement deletes all three.

analogy: Think of two accountants who each photocopy the ledger in the morning and work from their copy all day. That is Repeatable Read: each sees one fixed moment, and neither sees the other's work until it is filed. Read Committed is an accountant who makes a fresh copy before every calculation. Filing is COMMIT: the whole day's changes go into the real ledger at once, or none do. Write skew is both accountants approving a withdrawal against the same morning copy. Serializable adds a supervisor who notes which pages each accountant read and refuses to file a day's work that relied on a page the other one changed, so that accountant redoes the day from a new copy. The analogy breaks on cost: PostgreSQL copies nothing. A snapshot is a short list of transaction ids, the old row versions stay in the table until VACUUM removes them, and taking a snapshot costs microseconds.
in_your_world: Oracle at work runs at READ COMMITTED by default, and its SERIALIZABLE is snapshot isolation, so a limit check that reads a SUM and then writes (a merchant's daily cap, a refund ceiling, a card's velocity rule) can be broken by two concurrent requests at either level; lesson 3 has the fixes. On PostgreSQL the same check can run at SERIALIZABLE, and then 40001 is part of the API: in a Quarkus or Spring service the retry must wrap the whole @Transactional method, not one repository call. Every retry layer you already have, a Temporal activity retry, a Kafka redelivery, a client that resends after a timeout, is a retry after a possibly lost commit acknowledgement. So the charge, payout or refund it repeats needs an idempotency key that stays the same across attempts (the `payment_uid` of the course schema, or the key the card issuer's API takes), checked by a UNIQUE constraint in the same transaction as the write.
mistake: Reading "ACID" as "safe under concurrency". People believe it because the code sits inside one @Transactional method and every test runs one request at a time. A transaction makes the method's writes all-or-nothing and durable; at the default Read Committed it doesn't stop another transaction from reading the same rows in the meantime. The result is lost updates on counters and balances (lesson 2) and write skew on any rule over several rows (lesson 3), with no error anywhere. Find out which level you run at and which anomalies it allows on your database, then pick the fix: a relative update, a row lock, a constraint, or SERIALIZABLE with a retry of the whole transaction.

compare.title: The two withdrawals at SERIALIZABLE: Oracle and PostgreSQL

a.label: Oracle
a.title: Oracle: SERIALIZABLE is snapshot isolation
a.src:
-- in each session; :own is 109 in A, 209 in B
SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;

SELECT SUM(balance_minor) FROM accounts
WHERE customer_id = 9;              -- 10000 in both

UPDATE accounts
SET balance_minor = balance_minor - 8000
WHERE account_id = :own;            -- different rows

COMMIT;                             -- both succeed:
                                    -- the total is -6000

-- ORA-08177 "can't serialize access for this
-- transaction" comes only when both change
-- the SAME row

b.label: PostgreSQL 18
b.title: PostgreSQL: SERIALIZABLE is SSI
b.src:
-- in each session; :own is 109 in A, 209 in B
BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;

SELECT sum(balance_minor) FROM accounts
WHERE customer_id = 9;              -- 10000 in both

UPDATE accounts
SET balance_minor = balance_minor - 8000
WHERE account_id = :own;            -- different rows

COMMIT;                             -- one fails with
                                    -- 40001, read/write
                                    -- dependencies

-- retried from BEGIN, it reads 2000 and refuses;
-- PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ behaves like the
-- Oracle column

compare.note: The same keyword buys two different guarantees. Hermitage, Martin Kleppmann's test suite that runs the same interleavings against many databases, classifies Oracle's serializable as snapshot isolation: it prevents lost updates (P4) but not write skew (G2-item), which is PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ. PostgreSQL's SERIALIZABLE prevents every anomaly in the suite. Both databases default to READ COMMITTED with a snapshot per statement. So on Oracle, a rule across rows needs SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on a row every conflicting transaction must lock; on PostgreSQL you may choose between that lock and SERIALIZABLE with a retry loop.

worked.title: A charge that survives a lost acknowledgement

steps.say: The first version retries any SQLException. It looks careful, and it charges twice: if COMMIT reached the disk and the reply was lost, the second attempt inserts a second payment with a fresh `payment_uid` from the column's default.

Pick the key once per logical charge, before the first attempt, and send it with every attempt. The UNIQUE constraint on `payment_uid` turns a repeat into a no-op. When the insert returns no row, the charge already happened: read it back and return the same answer as the first attempt.

Sort the failures. A serialization failure or a deadlock means nothing happened: run the whole transaction again. A broken connection (SQLSTATE class 08) means the outcome is unknown, and with the key a retry is safe on a new connection. A constraint violation is a bug or a business refusal: retrying won't change it.

Put it together, with a growing pause between attempts. Anything outside the database, such as the receipt email, waits until the commit has succeeded; the outbox pattern in the Stream processing track makes that step reliable too.

lab.title: Stop the double withdrawal, then write the retry loop
steps: With Docker running, run the tests from the `labs` folder. Seven of the ten fail: the two `withdraw` tests where both withdrawals are Ivy's leave her total below zero, and the five `serializable` tests stop at a TODO.

`withdraw.sql` is one transaction. The tests run it in two sessions at once, one statement at a time, taking turns, and each session has its own one-row `withdrawal` table. Read the failure message: it lists every statement each session ran and what it returned.

Fix `withdraw.sql`. Either change its isolation level (the tests retry a session that fails with 40001, as your application would) or lock the rows the rule reads before the UPDATE. When it passes, try the other fix too.
Write `serializable` in `Retry.kt`: autocommit off, isolation SERIALIZABLE, run the work, commit, and on 40001 or 40P01 roll back and run the whole work again, up to `maxAttempts` attempts.
Run the tests until all ten pass. The last one runs two real withdrawals on two threads through your function, and makes both read Ivy's total before either writes.
hints: `BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;` is the one-line fix. In the log of the passing test, one session's COMMIT fails with 40001, and its retry updates nothing because its new snapshot sees the first withdrawal.

The lock version starts with `BEGIN;` (Read Committed), then `SELECT 1 FROM accounts WHERE customer_id = (SELECT customer_id FROM accounts JOIN withdrawal USING (account_id)) FOR UPDATE;`, then the same UPDATE. At REPEATABLE READ the same lock still ends in a 40001 for the waiting session: its snapshot is older than the commit it waited for.

In `serializable`, call `conn.commit()` inside the try, because SSI often reports the conflict at commit. Catch `SQLException`, call `conn.rollback()`, and rethrow unless `e.sqlState` is 40001 or 40P01 and attempts remain. Catch other exceptions separately: roll back and rethrow.

drill.title: The anomaly table, from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, fill in the table for PostgreSQL: for each of dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom, lost update and write skew, what happens at Read Committed, Repeatable Read and Serializable? Then write one line each on what Oracle's SERIALIZABLE and MySQL's REPEATABLE READ really are, and one sentence on when a retry after a failed COMMIT is safe.

answer.src:
Read Committed   Repeatable Read   Serializable
dirty read           never            never             never
non-repeatable read  happens          never             never
phantom              happens          never (in PG)     never
lost update          happens          error 40001       error 40001
write skew           happens          happens           error 40001

Oracle SERIALIZABLE:   snapshot isolation (like PG's REPEATABLE READ): write skew gets through
MySQL REPEATABLE READ: weaker than snapshot isolation: lost updates get through, no error

A retry after a failed COMMIT is safe only if the work carries an idempotency key checked by a
UNIQUE constraint, because the first COMMIT may have succeeded before the connection dropped.

recap: A transaction makes its changes permanent all at once, when its COMMIT record reaches the write-ahead log; an error, a ROLLBACK or a crash before that undoes all of them. One-row writes are atomic anyway: transactions are for changes that span several objects.

ACID: A is abortability, C is your rules (the database enforces only those you declared), I is whatever your level allows, D is a flushed commit record or replicas, with fine print. "ACID compliant" says almost nothing about isolation.
Read Committed takes a snapshot per statement. Repeatable Read keeps one per transaction (snapshot isolation) and turns a conflicting update into 40001.
Level names differ by vendor: Oracle's SERIALIZABLE is snapshot isolation, and MySQL's default REPEATABLE READ loses updates silently (Hermitage, Jepsen's 2023 MySQL analysis).
Write skew gets through Repeatable Read. PostgreSQL's SERIALIZABLE aborts one transaction with 40001, and you retry the whole transaction, reads included.
Retry only 40001, 40P01 and lost connections. A COMMIT whose reply was lost may have succeeded, so a retry is safe only with an idempotency key under a UNIQUE constraint.

quiz.q: At READ COMMITTED, transaction A runs `SELECT count(*) FROM ledger_entries WHERE account_id = 109` twice. Between the two, B inserts a ledger entry for 109 and commits. What does A's second count return?
options: The same as the first: a transaction sees one consistent state
One more than the first: each statement takes a new snapshot
An error, because rows changed under the transaction
The same as the first, unless A locked the rows with FOR UPDATE
quiz.why: Read Committed takes a snapshot at the start of each statement, so the second count includes B's committed row: a phantom. The first option describes Repeatable Read, where both counts would match. Neither level raises an error for a read.

quiz.q: A new datastore's home page says "Full ACID". Two concurrent requests each read a customer's total and then debit one of her accounts. What does the label tell you about them?
options: They behave as if they ran one after the other
Nothing yet: look up which anomalies its default isolation level allows
They can't lose an update, because the I in ACID forbids it
Nothing can go wrong as long as both run inside a transaction
quiz.why: ACID promises atomic, durable commits and an isolation level, without saying which. PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server default to Read Committed; MySQL's default loses updates; ParticleDB said "Full ACID" and ran at snapshot isolation. The first and third options describe serializability, which few databases give you by default, and a transaction alone doesn't stop concurrent reads of the same rows.

quiz.q: A REPEATABLE READ transaction fails on its third statement with SQLSTATE 40001, `could not serialize access due to concurrent update`. What should the application do?
options: Roll back and run the whole transaction again from BEGIN, reads included
Run the third statement again in the same transaction
Switch that one statement to READ COMMITTED and run it again
Nothing: PostgreSQL has already retried it
quiz.why: After an error the transaction is aborted and only ROLLBACK works. The retry has to redo the reads, because the error means they are out of date: rerunning the one statement would write a value computed from the old snapshot, which is the lost update the error just prevented.

quiz.q: An Oracle service enforces a merchant's daily limit across terminals: SELECT SUM(amount) for today, then INSERT the payment if it fits, at SERIALIZABLE. Two terminals pay at the same moment. What can happen?
options: Nothing bad: SERIALIZABLE prevents every anomaly
One INSERT always fails with ORA-08177
Both inserts commit and the limit is exceeded
The second SELECT waits until the first transaction commits
quiz.why: Oracle's SERIALIZABLE is snapshot isolation. Both transactions read the same sum from their snapshots and insert different rows, so no row is changed by both and nothing is reported: write skew. ORA-08177 appears only when two serializable transactions change the same row. Lock a row both must touch, such as the merchant row, with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE.

quiz.q: A Kotlin service sends COMMIT for a 42.00 charge, and the connection drops before the reply arrives (SQLSTATE 08006). What should it do?
options: Retry the whole transaction with a new payment_uid
Nothing: no reply means the charge failed
Send COMMIT again on a new connection
Retry with the same payment_uid, inserting with ON CONFLICT (payment_uid) DO NOTHING, and read the existing row if nothing was inserted
quiz.why: The commit record may have reached the disk before the connection broke, so the outcome is unknown. A retry with the key the client chose before the first attempt is safe either way: it inserts if the first attempt didn't commit, and finds its row if it did. A new uid turns a lost reply into a double charge. COMMIT on a new connection commits nothing, because the transaction belonged to the old one.

flashcards.front: When do a transaction's changes become permanent and visible to others?
flashcards.back: All at once, when its COMMIT record reaches the write-ahead log on disk. Before that no other session sees them, and a crash undoes them.

flashcards.front: What does the A in ACID really promise?
flashcards.back: Abortability: if anything fails before COMMIT, every write of the transaction is undone, so it can be retried. It says nothing about other sessions.

flashcards.front: Whose job is the C in ACID?
flashcards.back: The application's. The database enforces only the rules you declared: keys, foreign keys, CHECK, UNIQUE, exclusion constraints.

flashcards.front: What does a Read Committed statement read?
flashcards.back: A snapshot taken when that statement starts: everything committed by then. Two SELECTs in one transaction can disagree.
Two transactions read the same rows, each writes a different row, and together they break a rule each one checked. Repeatable Read allows it; Serializable aborts one.

flashcards.front: Is Oracle's SERIALIZABLE the same as PostgreSQL's?
flashcards.back: No. Oracle's is snapshot isolation, like PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ: write skew gets through.

flashcards.front: Why can a retry after a failed COMMIT charge a customer twice?
flashcards.back: The COMMIT may have reached the disk before the connection dropped. Send the same idempotency key on every attempt, under a UNIQUE constraint, so the repeat changes nothing.

terms.plain: A group of statements whose changes become permanent together at COMMIT, or not at all.
The A in ACID: a transaction can be aborted, and then none of its writes remain. Better called abortability.
The application's invariants. The database enforces only the ones declared as constraints.
The set of committed transactions a statement can see: everything committed before it was taken, nothing after, nothing uncommitted.
The setting that decides when a transaction's snapshot is taken and which conflicts PostgreSQL turns into errors.
Two transactions read the same rows, write different rows, and together break a rule that each checked.
PostgreSQL aborting a transaction because committing it would break its isolation level. The fix is to retry the whole transaction.
A value the client picks once per operation and sends with every attempt; a UNIQUE constraint turns a repeat into a no-op.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate says: "PostgreSQL is ACID, so concurrent requests can't corrupt our data, and retrying a failed transaction is always safe." Explain what ACID does and doesn't promise, and when each half of the claim is wrong.
explain_back.answer: ACID promises four things. Atomicity means a transaction that fails before COMMIT leaves no writes behind. Consistency means only the rules we declared as constraints are enforced. Durability means a committed transaction's commit record is on disk, with fine print around settings, disks and failover. Isolation means whatever our level allows, and PostgreSQL defaults to Read Committed. At that level two requests can both read a balance and both write a value computed from it, which loses an update, or both check a rule over several rows and each write a different row, which is write skew. Neither raises an error. So the first half is wrong unless we pick the right fix: a relative update, a row lock, a constraint, or SERIALIZABLE. The second half is wrong in two ways. Retrying a transaction that was aborted with 40001 or 40P01 is safe, but only if we rerun all of it, reads included. Retrying after a COMMIT whose reply was lost is not safe on its own, because the first attempt may have committed: the same charge goes in twice unless each attempt carries the same idempotency key under a UNIQUE constraint.

deeper.body:
Read Committed has a subtle rule for writes. When an `UPDATE` or `DELETE` finds that its target row was changed by a transaction that has just committed, it doesn't use its snapshot for that row. It rereads the newest version and checks the `WHERE` condition again; if the row still matches, the update applies to the new version. That's why `SET balance_minor = balance_minor - 1000` is safe at Read Committed (lesson 2). It also means one statement can see a mix: the new version of the rows it updates, and its snapshot for everything else. The PostgreSQL docs show a `DELETE` that misses a row because of it.

A transaction left open costs more than its locks. While it is open, its snapshot keeps every row version it might still need, so VACUUM can't remove dead versions anywhere in the database, and tables grow. Lesson 4 measures it. A service that forgets to commit, or a psql session left at `course=*#`, shows up as `idle in transaction` in `pg_stat_activity`; set `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` so PostgreSQL ends such sessions for you.

Long reports have a better option than plain Repeatable Read. `BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE, READ ONLY, DEFERRABLE` waits, if it must, until it can take a snapshot that no concurrent writer can invalidate, then runs with no risk of a serialization failure and no SSI bookkeeping.

Replication can weaken isolation that a single node gets right. Jepsen's 2023 MySQL analysis found anomalies under SERIALIZABLE on AWS RDS for MySQL, because a replication setting that preserves commit order was off by default there. Its 2025 analysis of Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL Multi-AZ clusters found histories that snapshot isolation forbids, because the primary and the replicas could disagree about the order of commits. A managed cluster isn't always as isolated as the engine inside it.

Other systems make the lost acknowledgement explicit. DynamoDB's `TransactWriteItems` takes a client token and treats a repeat within 10 minutes as the same transaction. CockroachDB returns 40003 when it can't tell whether a commit happened, and retries 40001 itself when the result is small enough to buffer.

*Designing Data-Intensive Applications*, 2nd edition, chapter 8, covers the meaning of ACID, single- and multi-object operations and the retry caveats in more depth.
